claim: The hippocampus is a brain area crucial for episodic memory in humans.
source: The hippocampus is a brain area crucial for episodic memory in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on human hippocampal function.

claim: Studies in rodents have highlighted the hippocampus's role in spatial learning, supported by the discovery of place cells.
source: In contrast, studies in rodents have highlighted its role in spatial learning, supported by the discovery of place cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature on rodent hippocampal function and place cells.

claim: Dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons are all place cells.
source: We show that dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons are all place cells, and do not respond to the tone when the animal is moving.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing spatial tuning properties of all recorded neurons.

claim: Dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons do not respond to the tone when the animal is moving.
source: We show that dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons are all place cells, and do not respond to the tone when the animal is moving.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing absence of CS-evoked responses during running.

claim: When the animal is inactive, the apparent tone-evoked responses reflect an arousal-mediated resumption of place-specific firing.
source: When the animal is inactive, the apparent tone-evoked responses reflect an arousal-mediated resumption of place-specific firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing CS responses only during inactivity, correlation with ripple cessation, and alignment with place field intensity.

claim: One of the main output stages of the hippocampus transmits only spatial information, even in this non-spatial task.
source: These results suggest that one of the main output stages of the hippocampus transmits only spatial information, even in this non-spatial task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings that all CA1 neurons are place cells and apparent non-spatial responses are arousal-mediated.

claim: The hippocampus plays a critical role in memory formation.
source: The hippocampus is a brain structure that is known to play a critical role in memory formation (Squire, 1992), but the scope and nature of hippocampal memory processing remains elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Squire, 1992.

claim: The discovery of place cells in rodents led to the hypothesis that the hippocampus forms a 'cognitive map' that is essential for spatial learning.
source: The discovery of place cells in rodents led to the hypothesis that the hippocampus forms a 'cognitive map' that is essential for spatial learning (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978.

claim: Human studies have indicated a more general role of the hippocampus in the formation of episodic memories.
source: In contrast, human studies have indicated a more general role of the hippocampus in the formation of episodic memories (Scoville and Milner, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Scoville and Milner, 1957.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in the dorsal CA1 area of the hippocampus can change their firing in response to arbitrary stimuli, both spatial and non-spatial.
source: In support of the latter view, electrophysiological studies in rodents have found that pyramidal neurons in the dorsal CA1 area of the hippocampus can change their firing in response to arbitrary stimuli, both spatial and non-spatial (Berger et al., 1976; Wood et al., 1999; Moita et al., 2003; Komorowski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berger et al., 1976; Wood et al., 1999; Moita et al., 2003; Komorowski et al., 2009.

claim: The functional significance of hippocampal responses to non-spatial stimuli remains controversial because many non-spatial tasks are studied in restrained animals or under circumstances where spatial and non-spatial influences on hippocampal firing cannot be unequivocally dissociated.
source: However, the functional significance of these observations remains controversial because many non-spatial tasks are studied in restrained animals or under circumstances where spatial and non-spatial influences on hippocampal firing cannot be unequivocally dissociated (O'Keefe, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Keefe, 1999.

claim: Learning the CS-US association in trace eyeblink conditioning has been shown to be hippocampally dependent in many species, including humans and rodents.
source: Learning the CS-US association has been shown to be hippocampally dependent in many species, including humans and rodents (Clark and Squire, 1998; Kim et al., 1995; Takehara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark and Squire, 1998; Kim et al., 1995; Takehara et al., 2003.

claim: Previous electrophysiological studies have found that dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons change their firing following the CS onset.
source: Previous electrophysiological studies have found that dorsal CA1 pyramidal neurons change their firing following the CS onset (Berger et al., 1976, 1983; Weiss et al., 1996; Weible et al., 2006), suggesting that these cells encode the non-spatial stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berger et al., 1976, 1983; Weiss et al., 1996; Weible et al., 2006.

claim: Previous electrophysiological studies did not characterize the spatial tuning properties of the recorded neurons.
source: However, these experiments did not characterize the spatial tuning properties of the recorded neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous studies.

claim: The study recorded from an average of 36 pyramidal cells per training session for a total of 1264 cells.
source: Using chronically implanted tetrode arrays, we recorded from pyramidal cells in the dorsal CA1 region of the hippocampus (an average of 36 cells per training session for a total of 1264).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: 10% of recorded cells significantly changed their firing rate following the CS onset (p<0.01).
source: Consistent with previous studies, we found that a subset of cells significantly changed their firing rate following the CS onset (p<0.01 for 10% of cells, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: None of the recorded cells respond consistently to the CS onset.
source: However, an analysis of single-trial responses reveals that these cell-level statistics belie a high trial-to-trial variability, and none of the recorded cells respond consistently to the CS onset (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Cells that were active in the environment had directional place fields distributed throughout the linear track.
source: Cells that were active in the environment had directional place fields distributed throughout the linear track (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The remaining cells had low firing rates everywhere, consistent with place cells that lack a place field in this environment.
source: The remaining cells had low firing rates everywhere, consistent with place cells that lack a place field in this environment.
evidence: This is an inference based on observed firing patterns.

claim: A cell's spatial tuning exerts a strong influence on its response to non-spatial stimuli.
source: These spatial firing rate maps—which were constructed with eyeblink trials omitted—reveal that a cell's spatial tuning exerts a strong influence on its response to non-spatial stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between place field intensity and CS-evoked firing.

claim: The CS evokes an increase in firing when delivered within a cell's place field, and silences the cell when delivered outside its place field.
source: Overall, we find that the CS evokes an increase in firing when delivered within a cell's place field, and silences the cell when delivered outside its place field (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: The correlation between CS-evoked firing and place field intensity holds at the single-cell level.
source: This correlation between CS-evoked firing and place field intensity also holds at the single-cell level (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There are no CA1 neurons that respond consistently to the CS in a space-invariant fashion.
source: These observations indicate that there are no CA1 neurons that respond consistently to the CS in a space-invariant fashion.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing spatial modulation of all CS responses.

claim: CS-evoked changes in firing rate are absent when the animal is running.
source: Surprisingly, we find the opposite: CS-evoked changes in firing rate are absent when the animal is running (Figure 3A) and occur only when the animal is inactive (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: CS-evoked changes in firing rate occur only when the animal is inactive.
source: Surprisingly, we find the opposite: CS-evoked changes in firing rate are absent when the animal is running (Figure 3A) and occur only when the animal is inactive (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The lack of CS-evoked changes while running is not accompanied by an impairment of task performance.
source: Importantly, the lack of CS-evoked changes while running is not accompanied by an impairment of task performance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When the animal is sitting, the CS-evoked change in firing reflects the fact that the pre-trial firing rates differ from the spatially predicted rates.
source: When the animal is sitting, the CS-evoked change in firing actually reflects the fact that the pre-trial firing rates differ from the spatially predicted rates (Figure 3C, grey markers).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: After the CS onset, firing rates re-align with the place field intensity at the present location.
source: After the CS onset, firing rates re-align with the place field intensity at the present location (Figure 3C, blue markers).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When the animal is sitting, ripples spontaneously occur during the pre-trial period, and abruptly cease following the CS onset.
source: We find that when the animal is sitting, ripples spontaneously occur during the pre-trial period, and abruptly cease following the CS onset (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CS-evoked changes in firing rate are more pronounced in trials with detected ripples.
source: Furthermore, CS-evoked changes in firing rate are more pronounced in trials with detected ripples (Figure 4B) and the firing of these cells outside their place fields is closely associated with the ripple events (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The firing of cells outside their place fields is closely associated with ripple events.
source: Furthermore, CS-evoked changes in firing rate are more pronounced in trials with detected ripples (Figure 4B) and the firing of these cells outside their place fields is closely associated with the ripple events (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The CS triggers an arousal response that leads to a resumption of place cell firing.
source: These observations suggest that the animal is indeed in a state of quiet wakefulness during 'sitting' trials, and that the CS triggers an arousal response that leads to a resumption of place cell firing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations about ripples, firing rates, and brain state.

claim: Both the CS and US can evoke a sustained alignment of theta phase, but only in one out of three animals.
source: Under these conditions, we found that both the CS and US can evoke a sustained alignment of theta phase, but only in one out of three animals (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: When theta phase alignment did occur, the new phase remained highly correlated with the pre-stimulus phase.
source: Even when theta phase alignment did occur, the new phase remained highly correlated with the pre-stimulus phase (Figure 5E), indicating that the observed alignment is due to a subtle phase shift rather than a reset of the theta rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The observed theta phase alignment is due to a subtle phase shift rather than a reset of the theta rhythm.
source: Even when theta phase alignment did occur, the new phase remained highly correlated with the pre-stimulus phase (Figure 5E), indicating that the observed alignment is due to a subtle phase shift rather than a reset of the theta rhythm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation analysis of pre- and post-stimulus theta phase.

claim: It is possible for the eyeblink stimuli to perturb ongoing theta oscillations, but the absence of this perturbation in two out of three animals shows that it is not necessary to perform the task.
source: These results confirm that it is possible for the eyeblink stimuli to perturb ongoing theta oscillations, but the absence of this perturbation in two out of three animals shows that it is not necessary to perform the task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability in theta phase alignment across animals.

claim: None of the 1264 pyramidal cells responded in a purely non-spatial manner.
source: The simplest form of non-spatial coding would be a purely non-spatial CS cell (Figure 6A) that exhibits a consistent change in firing to the CS independent of the animal's location. None of the 1264 pyramidal cells responded in this purely non-spatial manner.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The lack of CS responses when the animal is running is not consistent with the CS-place cell model.
source: At first glance, our data appear to fit this model—the CS responses of place cells are gated by their place fields (Figure 2)—but our key observation is that CS-evoked changes in firing rate disappear when the animal is running (Figure 3). This new finding rejects the conjunctive model because these cells can no longer encode the CS-place conjunction in this behavioral state.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing absence of CS responses during running.

claim: Place cells exhibit place-specific firing only when the animal is moving or alert, and exhibit a different pattern of firing when the animal is in a state of quiet wakefulness.
source: In particular, place cells exhibit place-specific firing only when the animal is moving or alert, and exhibit a different pattern of firing when the animal is in a state of quiet wakefulness.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about place cell behavior.

claim: If the CS were able to trigger an arousal response, this would manifest as an increase in firing within a cell's place field and a decrease in firing outside the place field.
source: If the CS were able to trigger an arousal response, this would manifest as an increase in firing within a cell's place field (due to activation of place-specific firing) and a decrease in firing outside the place field (due to cessation of ripple-related firing).
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on known properties of place cells and brain states.

claim: In sitting animals, the CS activates place-specific firing, silences out-of-field firing, and abolishes ripples.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we find that in sitting animals, the CS indeed activates place-specific firing, silences out-of-field firing, and abolishes ripples.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figures 3 and 4.

claim: When the animal is already alert, such as during running, no additional modulation beyond normal place field firing is observed.
source: When the animal is already alert, such as during running, we observe no additional modulation beyond normal place field firing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Figure 3A.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation of the experimental data is that dorsal CA1 neurons are all place cells and the apparent responses to the non-spatial stimuli are due to an arousal-mediated resumption of place-specific firing.
source: Hence the most parsimonious explanation of the experimental data is that dorsal CA1 neurons are all place cells and the apparent responses to the non-spatial stimuli are due to an arousal-mediated resumption of place-specific firing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental observations.

claim: Studies of inactive subjects in a fixed location would find that a subset of cells—those with a place field overlapping the experiment location—consistently increase their firing following the stimulus presentation.
source: Studies of inactive subjects in a fixed location, such as those with restrained animals (Berger et al., 1983; Weiss et al., 1996; Weible et al., 2006), would find that a subset of cells—those with a place field overlapping the experiment location—consistently increase their firing following the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings applied to previous experimental paradigms.

claim: Any salient stimulus should be able to evoke hippocampal responses, regardless of whether the task is hippocampally dependent.
source: In particular, any salient stimulus should be able to evoke these hippocampal responses, regardless of whether the task is hippocampally dependent (Berger et al., 1983; Moita et al., 2003; Abe et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Berger et al., 1983; Moita et al., 2003; Abe et al., 2014.

claim: The salience of the stimulus may change as the subject learns the predictive power of the stimulus, producing a stereotyped evolution of hippocampal activity across learning.
source: The salience of the stimulus, and hence its ability to trigger alertness, may change as the subject learns the predictive power of the stimulus, producing a stereotyped evolution of hippocampal activity across learning (McEchron and Disterhoft, 1997).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to McEchron and Disterhoft, 1997.

claim: Manipulations that decrease the salience of the CS, such as habituation to the unpaired stimuli presented to control animals, would reduce the apparent response.
source: On the other hand, manipulations that decrease the salience of the CS, such as habituation to the unpaired stimuli presented to control animals, would reduce the apparent response (Berger et al., 1976; Weiss et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by citations to Berger et al., 1976; Weiss et al., 1996.

claim: Previous studies have reported that the CS can reset the phase of hippocampal theta oscillations.
source: Previous studies have also reported that the CS can reset the phase of hippocampal theta oscillations (Nokia et al., 2010; Darling et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nokia et al., 2010; Darling et al., 2011.

claim: The CS onset is not encoded by theta phase reset.
source: Given the lack of CS-evoked firing rate changes while running, could the CS onset be encoded by this phase reset instead? Analogous to previous studies, we find evidence for an alignment of theta phase to the CS onset. However, a direct comparison of pre- and post-stimulus phase reveals that this effect is due to a slight perturbation of the ongoing theta phase (Figure 5). In particular, this analysis rejects the notion of theta reset to a specific phase.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the theta phase continuity analysis.

claim: Theta phase perturbation is present in only one out of three animals, indicating that it is not necessary for performing the task.
source: Furthermore, this phase perturbation is present in only one out of three animals, indicating that it is not necessary for performing the task.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability in theta phase effects across animals.

claim: There is no evidence that theta phase precession was affected by the CS onset.
source: Moreover, we did not find evidence that theta phase precession was affected by the CS onset (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The analysis does not rule out the possibility that the CS may modulate the degree of theta phase-locking across brain areas.
source: Note, however, that this analysis does not rule out the possibility that the CS may modulate the degree of theta phase-locking across brain areas.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analysis.

claim: Extensive lesion studies have demonstrated the critical importance of the hippocampus in trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Finally, extensive lesion studies have demonstrated the critical importance of the hippocampus in trace eyeblink conditioning (Kim et al., 1995; Takehara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kim et al., 1995; Takehara et al., 2003.

claim: CS-evoked changes in dorsal CA1 firing rates and theta phase are not necessary for task performance.
source: We found that CS-evoked changes in dorsal CA1 firing rates and theta phase are not necessary for task performance—these responses are absent during running, but performance is not impaired—yet dorsally restricted lesions still produce learning deficits (Takehara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison with lesion studies.

claim: Dorsally restricted hippocampal lesions produce learning deficits in trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: We found that CS-evoked changes in dorsal CA1 firing rates and theta phase are not necessary for task performance—these responses are absent during running, but performance is not impaired—yet dorsally restricted lesions still produce learning deficits (Takehara et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Takehara et al., 2003.

claim: Dorsal hippocampal lesions may disrupt activity in other hippocampal areas (e.g. ventral CA1), which may contain genuinely CS-responsive neurons.
source: (1) Dorsal hippocampal lesions may disrupt activity in other hippocampal areas (e.g. ventral CA1), which may contain genuinely CS-responsive neurons.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the discrepancy between the current findings and lesion studies.

claim: The encoding of the CS may be more subtle than changes in firing rate, but still detectable by postsynaptic targets.
source: (2) The encoding of the CS may be more subtle than changes in firing rate, but still detectable by postsynaptic targets.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the discrepancy between the current findings and lesion studies.

claim: The critical engagement of the hippocampus may not occur only during the trial itself.
source: (3) The critical engagement of the hippocampus may not occur only during the trial itself. Memory consolidation is hippocampally dependent and proceeds without additional training (Takehara et al., 2003; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008), indicating that some eyeblink-related activity occurs well after the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Takehara et al., 2003; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008.

claim: Memory consolidation is hippocampally dependent and proceeds without additional training.
source: Memory consolidation is hippocampally dependent and proceeds without additional training (Takehara et al., 2003; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008), indicating that some eyeblink-related activity occurs well after the stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Takehara et al., 2003; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008.

claim: The presence of ongoing place-specific firing may be necessary for learning space-invariant responses.
source: (4) Even though spatial information may appear irrelevant in this task, the presence of ongoing place-specific firing may still be necessary for learning space-invariant responses.
evidence: This is speculation about possible explanations for the discrepancy between the current findings and lesion studies.

claim: Awareness of the context may be necessary for the animal to attend to the appropriate stimuli.
source: For example, awareness of the context may be necessary for the animal to attend to the appropriate stimuli, or learning a context-dependent association may be a necessary stepping-stone to developing a space-invariant association (Nadel and Willner, 1980).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Nadel and Willner, 1980.

claim: Learning a context-dependent association may be a necessary stepping-stone to developing a space-invariant association.
source: For example, awareness of the context may be necessary for the animal to attend to the appropriate stimuli, or learning a context-dependent association may be a necessary stepping-stone to developing a space-invariant association (Nadel and Willner, 1980).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Nadel and Willner, 1980.

claim: The dorsal hippocampus transmits exclusively spatial signals, even in a hippocampally dependent non-spatial task.
source: These findings suggest that the dorsal hippocampus transmits exclusively spatial signals, even in a hippocampally dependent non-spatial task, and constrain the ways in which it may contribute to memory processing.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all experimental findings.

claim: It is important to account for brain state in studies where alertness changes may confound the observed selectivity to experimental stimuli.
source: These experiments also highlight the importance of accounting for brain state in studies where alertness changes may confound the observed selectivity to experimental stimuli.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about experimental methodology drawn from the findings.

claim: Three male Long-Evans rats, 3–5 months old at the time of surgery, were used in the study.
source: We recorded from three male Long-Evans rats, 3–5 months old at the time of surgery.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Each animal was chronically implanted with a differential pair of EMG recording wires in the left eyelid muscle, a pair of bipolar stimulation electrodes in the same area, and a microdrive array that allowed independent adjustment of 24 tetrodes.
source: We chronically implanted each animal with a differential pair of EMG recording wires in the left eyelid muscle, a pair of bipolar stimulation electrodes in the same area, and a microdrive array that allowed independent adjustment of 24 tetrodes.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: In two animals (A and B), tetrodes were targeted to the right dorsal hippocampus.
source: In two animals (A and B), these tetrodes were targeted to the right dorsal hippocampus; animal C received a bilateral implant targeting the dorsal hippocampus in both hemispheres.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Animal C received a bilateral implant targeting the dorsal hippocampus in both hemispheres.
source: In two animals (A and B), these tetrodes were targeted to the right dorsal hippocampus; animal C received a bilateral implant targeting the dorsal hippocampus in both hemispheres.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: A 250 ms, 5 kHz tone was used as the CS.
source: We used a 250 ms, 5 kHz tone as the CS, a 250 ms stimulus-free trace interval, and 10 ms bipolar stimulation of the eyelid muscle as the US.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: A 250 ms stimulus-free trace interval was used.
source: We used a 250 ms, 5 kHz tone as the CS, a 250 ms stimulus-free trace interval, and 10 ms bipolar stimulation of the eyelid muscle as the US.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: 10 ms bipolar stimulation of the eyelid muscle was used as the US.
source: We used a 250 ms, 5 kHz tone as the CS, a 250 ms stimulus-free trace interval, and 10 ms bipolar stimulation of the eyelid muscle as the US.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: Lesion studies in rats have shown that a 250 ms trace interval requires the hippocampus for successful acquisition.
source: Lesion studies in rats have shown that this trace interval requires the hippocampus for successful acquisition (Weiss et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Weiss et al., 1999.

claim: Animals received between 38 and 186 eyeblink trials per training session (an average of 109).
source: Animals received between 38 and 186 eyeblink trials per training session (an average of 109), depending on how much they ran on the track.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: All animals received two training sessions per day, at the beginning and end of the 12-hr light cycle.
source: All animals received two training sessions per day, at the beginning and end of the 12-hr light cycle.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: 1585 single units were identified, of which 1264 were deemed to be putative pyramidal cells.
source: These criteria identified 1585 single units, of which 1264 we deemed to be putative pyramidal cells based on firing rate (<4 Hz), spike width (>0.25 ms), and bursting (>5% of inter-spike intervals are <10 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data and analysis methods.

claim: Putative pyramidal cells were identified based on firing rate (<4 Hz), spike width (>0.25 ms), and bursting (>5% of inter-spike intervals are <10 ms).
source: These criteria identified 1585 single units, of which 1264 we deemed to be putative pyramidal cells based on firing rate (<4 Hz), spike width (>0.25 ms), and bursting (>5% of inter-spike intervals are <10 ms).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental methods.

claim: The study estimates that only 400–500 unique pyramidal cells were recorded.
source: Each of these 1264 units is treated independently in our analysis, even though several are likely to be repeated observations of the same neuron. We estimate that we recorded only 400–500 unique pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the analysis of recorded units.

claim: 38% of cells were not active in this environment (i.e. did not have a place field with peak > 2 Hz).
source: We found that 38% of cells were not active in this environment (i.e. did not have a place field with peak > 2 Hz), but this underestimates the actual fraction of silent cells, as we are unable to reliably cluster single units with an overall firing rate < 0.01 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: The 38% figure underestimates the actual fraction of silent cells, as the study was unable to reliably cluster single units with an overall firing rate < 0.01 Hz.
source: We found that 38% of cells were not active in this environment (i.e. did not have a place field with peak > 2 Hz), but this underestimates the actual fraction of silent cells, as we are unable to reliably cluster single units with an overall firing rate < 0.01 Hz.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the analysis methods.

claim: 87 cells increased their firing rate following the CS onset.
source: We found 123 cells (10% of all pyramidal cells) that were significant at a p<0.01 level. Of these, 87 increased their firing rate and 36 decreased their firing rate.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: 36 cells decreased their firing rate following the CS onset.
source: We found 123 cells (10% of all pyramidal cells) that were significant at a p<0.01 level. Of these, 87 increased their firing rate and 36 decreased their firing rate.
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental data.

claim: The statistical test for CS response should be interpreted as a heuristic measure only, as the influences of spatial tuning and brain state violate the test's assumption that samples are independent and identically distributed.
source: However, this statistical test should be interpreted as a heuristic measure only, as the influences of spatial tuning and brain state violate the test's assumption that samples are independent and identically distributed.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the statistical analysis.
